entries.b3df8dff24b55b338467cace93a957ecfe4cd4ad: <div sID="gen10407" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="6" osisID="Ps.6" sID="Ps.6"/> <div eID="gen10407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10408" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10409" type="x-p"/> David was a weeping prophet as well as Jeremiah, and this psalm is one of his lamentations: either it was penned in a time, or at least calculated for a time, of great trouble, both outward and inward. Is any afflicted? Is any sick? Let him sing this psalm. The method of this psalm is very observable, and what we shall often meet with. He begins with doleful complaints, but ends with joyful praises; like Hannah, who went to prayer with a sorrowful spirit, but, when she had prayed, went her way, and her countenance was no more sad. Three things the psalmist is here complaining of:—1. Sickness of body. 2. Trouble of mind, arising from the sense of sin, the meritorious cause of pain and sickness. 3. The insults of his enemies upon occasion of both. Now here, I. He pours out his complaints before God, deprecates his wrath, and begs earnestly for the return of his favour, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.1-Ps.6.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. He assures himself of an answer of peace, shortly, to his full satisfaction, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.8-Ps.6.10">ver. 8-10</reference>. This psalm is like the book of Job.
entries.51a779eab04c556c0d73b7028136c872396b10fc: <div eID="gen10409" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10408" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Complaints.</title> <div sID="gen10410" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , rebuke me not in thine anger, neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure. 2 Have mercy upon me, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> ; for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> weak: <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , heal me; for my bones are vexed. <hi type="super">3</hi> My soul is also sore vexed: but thou, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , how long? <hi type="super">4</hi> Return, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , deliver my soul: oh save me for thy mercies' sake. <hi type="super">5</hi> For in death <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no remembrance of thee: in the grave who shall give thee thanks? <hi type="super">6</hi> I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears. <hi type="super">7</hi> Mine eye is consumed because of grief; it waxeth old because of all mine enemies. <div eID="gen10410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10411" type="x-p"/> These verses speak the language of a heart truly humbled under humbling providences, of a broken and contrite spirit under great afflictions, sent on purpose to awaken conscience and mortify corruption. Those heap up wrath who cry not when God binds them; but those are getting ready for mercy who, under God's rebukes, sow in tears, as David does here. Let us observe here, <div eID="gen10411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10412" type="x-p"/> I. The representation he makes to God of his grievances. He pours out his complaint before him. Whither else should a child go with his complaints, but to his father? 1. He complains of bodily pain and sickness (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">My bones are vexed.</hi> His bones and his flesh, like Job's, were touched. Though David was a king, yet he was sick and pained; his imperial crown could not keep his head from aching. Great men are men, and subject to the common calamities of human life. Though David was a stout man, a man of war from his youth, yet this could not secure him from distempers, which will soon make even the strong men to bow themselves. Though David was a good man, yet neither could his goodness keep him in health. <hi type="italic">Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick.</hi> Let this help to reconcile us to pain and sickness, that it has been the lot of some of the best saints, and that we are directed and encouraged by their example to show before God our trouble in that case, who <hi type="italic">is for the body,</hi> and takes cognizance of its ailments. 2. He complains of inward trouble: <hi type="italic">My soul is also sorely vexed;</hi> and that is much more grievous than the vexation of the bones. <hi type="italic">The spirit of a man will sustain his infirmity,</hi> if that be in good plight; but, if that be wounded, the grievance is intolerable. David's sickness brought his sin to his remembrance, and he looked upon it as a token of God's displeasure against him; that was the vexation of his soul; that made him cry, <hi type="italic">I am weak, heal me.</hi> It is a sad thing for a man to have his bones and his soul vexed at the same time; but this has been sometimes the lot of God's own people: nay, and this completed his complicated trouble, that it was continued upon him a great while, which is here intimated in that expostulation (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.3">v. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou, O Lord! how long?</hi> To the living God we must, at such a time, address ourselves, who is the only physician both of body and mind, and not to the Assyrians, not to the god of Ekron. <div eID="gen10412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10413" type="x-p"/> II. The impression which his troubles made upon him. They lay very heavily; he <hi type="italic">groaned till he was weary,</hi> wept till he <hi type="italic">made his bed to swim,</hi> and <hi type="italic">watered his couch</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.6">v. 6</reference>), wept till he had almost wept his eyes out (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">My eye is consumed because of grief.</hi> David had more courage and consideration than to mourn thus for any outward affliction; but, when sin sat heavily upon his conscience and he was made to possess his iniquities, when his soul was wounded with the sense of God's wrath and his withdrawings from him, then he thus grieves and mourns in secret, and even his soul refuses to be comforted. This not only kept his eyes waking, but kept his eyes weeping. Note, 1. It has often been the lot of the best of men to be men of sorrows; our Lord Jesus himself was so. Our way lies through a vale of tears, and we must accommodate ourselves to the temper of the climate. 2. It well becomes the greatest spirits to be tender, and to relent, under the tokens of God's displeasure. David, who could face Goliath himself and many another threatening enemy with an undaunted bravery, yet melts into tears at the remembrance of sin and under the apprehensions of divine wrath; and it was no diminution at all to his character to do so. 3. True penitents weep in their retirements. The Pharisees disguised their faces, that they might <hi type="italic">appear unto men to mourn;</hi> but David mourned in the night upon the bed where he lay communing with his own heart, and no eye was a witness to his grief, but the eye of him who is all eye. Peter went out, covered his face, and wept. 4. Sorrow for sin ought to be great sorrow; so David's was; he wept so bitterly, so abundantly, that he watered his couch. 5. The triumphs of wicked men in the sorrows of the saints add very much to their grief. David's eye waxed old because of his enemies, who rejoiced in his afflictions and put bad constructions upon his tears. In this great sorrow David was a type of Christ, who often wept, and who cried out, <hi type="italic">My soul is exceedingly sorrowful,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.5.7">Heb. v. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen10413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10414" type="x-p"/> III. The petitions which he offers up to God in this sorrowful and distressed state. 1. That which he dreads as the greatest evil is the anger of God. This was the wormwood and the gall in the affliction and the misery; it was the infusion of this that made it indeed a bitter cup; and therefore he prays (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.1">v. 1</reference>), <hi type="italic">O Lord! rebuke me not in thy anger,</hi> though I have deserved it, <hi type="italic">neither chasten me in thy hot displeasure.</hi> He does not pray, "Lord, rebuke me not; Lord, chasten me not;" for, <hi type="italic">as many as God loves he rebukes and chastens, as a father the son in whom he delights.</hi> He can bear the rebuke and chastening well enough if God, at the same time, lift up the light of his countenance upon him and by his Spirit make him to hear the joy and gladness of his loving-kindness; the affliction of his body will be tolerable if he have but comfort in his soul. No matter though sickness make his bones ache, if God's wrath do not make his heart ache; therefore his prayer is, "<hi type="italic">Lord, rebuke me not in thy wrath;</hi> let me not lie under the impressions of that, for that will sink me." Herein David was a type of Christ, whose sorest complaint, in his sufferings, was of the trouble of his soul and of the suspension of his Father's smiles. He never so much as whispered a complaint of the rage of his enemies—"Why do they crucify me?" or the unkindness of his friends—"Why do they desert me?" But he <hi type="italic">cried with a loud voice, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?</hi> Let us thus deprecate the wrath of God more than any outward trouble whatsoever and always beware of treasuring up wrath against a day of affliction. 2. That which he desires as the greatest good, and which would be to him the restoration of all good, is the favour and friendship of God. He prays, (1.) That God would pity him and look upon him with compassion. He thinks himself very miserable, and misery is the proper object of mercy. Hence he prays, "<hi type="italic">Have mercy upon me, O Lord!</hi> in wrath remember mercy, and deal not with me in strict justice." (2.) That God would pardon his sins; for that is the proper act of mercy, and is often chiefly intended in that petition, <hi type="italic">Have mercy upon me.</hi> (3.) That God would put forth his power for his relief: "<hi type="italic">Lord, heal me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.2">v. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">save me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.4">v. 4</reference>), speak the word, and I shall be whole, and all will be well." (4.) That he would be at peace with him: "<hi type="italic">Return, O Lord!</hi> receive me into thy favour again, and be reconciled to me. Thou hast seemed to depart from me and neglect me, nay, to set thyself at a distance, as one angry; but now, Lord, return and show thyself nigh to me." (5.) That he would especially preserve the inward man and the interests of that, whatever might become of the body: "<hi type="italic">O Lord! deliver my soul</hi> from sinning, from sinking, from perishing for ever." It is an unspeakable privilege that we have a God to go to in our afflictions, and it is our duty to go to him, and thus to wrestle with him, and we shall not seek in vain. <div eID="gen10414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10415" type="x-p"/> IV. The pleas with which he enforces his petitions, not to move God (he knows our cause and the true merits of it better than we can state them), but to move himself. 1. He pleads God's mercy; and thence we take some of our best encouragements in prayer: <hi type="italic">Save me, for thy mercies' sake.</hi> 3. He pleads God's glory (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.5">v. 5</reference>): "<hi type="italic">For in death there is no remembrance of thee.</hi> Lord, if thou deliver me and comfort me, I will not only give thee thanks for my deliverance, and stir up others to join with me in these thanksgivings, but I will spend the new life thou shalt entrust me with in thy service and to thy glory, and all the remainder of my days I will preserve a grateful remembrance of thy favours to me, and be quickened thereby in all instances of service to thee; but, if I die, I shall be cut short of that opportunity of honouring thee and doing good to others, for <hi type="italic">in the grave who will give the thanks?</hi>" Not but that separate souls live and act, and the souls of the faithful joyfully remember God and give thanks to him. But, (1.) In the second death (which perhaps David, being now troubled in soul under the wrath of God, had some dreadful apprehensions of) there is no pleasing remembrance of God; devils and damned spirits blaspheme him and do not praise him. "Lord, let me not lie always under this wrath, for that is <hi type="italic">sheol,</hi> it is <hi type="italic">hell</hi> itself, and lays me under an everlasting disability to praise thee." Those that sincerely seek God's glory, and desire and delight to praise him, may pray in faith, "Lord, send me not to that dreadful place, where there is no devout remembrance of thee, nor are any thanks given to thee." (2.) Even the death of the body puts an end to our opportunity and capacity of glorifying God in this world, and serving the interests of his kingdom among men by opposing the powers of darkness and bringing many on this earth to know God and devote themselves to him. Some have maintained that the joys of the saints in heaven are more desirable, infinitely more so, than the comforts of saints on earth; yet the services of saints on earth, especially such eminent ones as David was, are more laudable, and redound more to the glory of the divine grace, than the services of the saints in heaven, who are not employed in maintaining the war against sin and Satan, nor in edifying the body of Christ. Courtiers in the royal presence are most happy, but soldiers in the field are more useful; and therefore we may, with good reason, pray that if it be the will of God, and he has any further work for us or our friends to do in this world, he will yet spare us, or them, to serve him. To depart and be with Christ is most happy for the saints themselves; but for them to abide in the flesh is more profitable for the church. This David had an eye to when he pleaded this, <hi type="italic">In the grave who shall give thee thanks?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.30.9">Ps. xxx. 9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.10">lxxxviii. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.115.17">cxv. 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.38.18">Isa. xxxviii. 18</reference>. And this Christ had an eye to when he said, <hi type="italic">I pray not that thou shouldst take them out of the world.</hi> <div eID="gen10415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10416" type="x-p"/> We should sing <reference osisRef="Ps.6.1-Ps.6.7">these verses</reference> with a deep sense of the terrors of God's wrath, which we should therefore dread and deprecate above any thing; and with thankfulness if this be not our condition, and compassion to those who are thus afflicted: if we be thus troubled, let it comfort us that our case is not without precedent, nor, if we humble ourselves and pray, as David did, shall it be long without redress.
entries.6db0c138b1555867dd59a9705ef7bcf943bb8c68: <div eID="gen10416" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Confidence in God.</title> <div sID="gen10417" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity; for the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath heard the voice of my weeping. <hi type="super">9</hi> The <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath heard my supplication; the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> will receive my prayer. <hi type="super">10</hi> Let all mine enemies be ashamed and sore vexed: let them return <hi type="italic">and</hi> be ashamed suddenly. <div eID="gen10417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10418" type="x-p"/> What a sudden change is here for the better! He that was groaning, and weeping, and giving up all for gone (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.6-Ps.6.7">v. 6, 7</reference>), here looks and speaks very pleasantly. Having made his requests known to God, and lodged his case with him, he is very confident the issue will be good and his sorrow is turned into joy. <div eID="gen10418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10419" type="x-p"/> I. He distinguishes himself from the wicked and ungodly, and fortifies himself against their insults (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity.</hi> When he was in the depth of his distress, 1. He was afraid that God's wrath against him would give him his portion with the workers of iniquity; but now that this cloud of melancholy had blown over he was assured that his soul would not be gathered with sinners, for they are not his people. He began to suspect himself to be one of them because of the heavy pressures of God's wrath upon him; but now that all his fears were silenced he bade them depart, knowing that his lot was among the chosen. 2. The workers of iniquity had teased him, and taunted him, and asked him, "Where is thy God?" triumphing in his despondency and despair; but now he had wherewith to answer those that reproached him, for God, who was about to return in mercy to him, had now comforted his spirit and would shortly complete his deliverance. 3. Perhaps they had tempted him to do as they did, to quit his religion and betake himself for ease to the pleasures of sin. But now, "<hi type="italic">depart from me;</hi> I will never lend an ear to your counsel; you would have had me to curse God and die, but I will bless him and live." This good use we should make of God's mercies to us, we should thereby have our resolution strengthened never to have any thing more to do with sin and sinners. David was a king, and he takes this occasion to renew his purpose of using his power for the suppression of sin and the reformation of manners, <reference osisRef="Ps.75.4">Ps. lxxv. 4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.101.3">ci. 3</reference>. When God has done great things for us, this should put us upon studying what we shall do for him. Our Lord Jesus seems to borrow these words from the mouth of his father David, when, having all judgment committed to him, he shall say, <hi type="italic">Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.13.27">Luke xiii. 27</reference>), and so teaches us to say so now, <reference osisRef="Ps.119.115">Ps. cxix. 115</reference>. <div eID="gen10419" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10420" type="x-p"/> II. He assures himself that God was, and would be, propitious to him, notwithstanding the present intimations of wrath which he was under. 1. He is confident of a gracious answer to this prayer which he is now making. While he is yet speaking, he is aware that God hears (as <reference osisRef="Isa.65.24">Isa. lxv. 24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.20">Dan. ix. 20</reference>), and therefore speaks of it as a thing done, and repeats it with an air of triumph, "<hi type="italic">The Lord hath heard</hi>" (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.8">v. 8</reference>), and again (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.9">v. 9</reference>), "<hi type="italic">The Lord hath heard.</hi>" By the workings of God's grace upon his heart he knew his prayer was graciously accepted, and therefore did not doubt but it would in due time be effectually answered. His tears had a voice, a loud voice, in the ears of the God of mercy: <hi type="italic">The Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.</hi> Silent tears are not speechless ones. His prayers were cries to God: "<hi type="italic">The Lord has heard the voice of my supplication,</hi> has put his <hi type="italic">Fiat—Let it be done,</hi> to my petitions, and so it will appear shortly." 2. Thence he infers the like favourable audience of all his other prayers: "He <hi type="italic">has heard the voice of my supplication,</hi> and therefore he <hi type="italic">will receive my prayer;</hi> for he gives, and does not upbraid with former grants." <div eID="gen10420" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10421" type="x-p"/> III. He either prays for the conversion or predicts the destruction of his enemies and persecutors, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.10">v. 10</reference>. 1. It may very well be taken as a prayer for their conversion: "Let them all be ashamed of the opposition they have given me and the censures they have passed upon me. Let them be (as all true penitents are) vexed at themselves for their own folly; let them return to a better temper and disposition of mind, and let them be ashamed of what they have done against me and take shame to themselves." 2. If they be not converted, it is a prediction of their confusion and ruin. <hi type="italic">They shall be ashamed and sorely vexed</hi> (so it maybe read), and that justly. They rejoiced that David was vexed (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.2-Ps.6.3">v. 2, 3</reference>), and therefore, as usually happens, the evil returns upon themselves; they also shall be sorely vexed. Those that will not give glory to God shall have their faces filled with everlasting shame. <div eID="gen10421" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10422" type="x-p"/> In singing this, and praying over it, we must give glory to God, as a God ready to hear prayer, must own his goodness to us in hearing our prayers, and must encourage ourselves to wait upon him and to trust in him in the greatest straits and difficulties.  <chapter eID="Ps.6"/> <div eID="gen10422" type="x-p"/>

entries.3fcb37119f1faad482589e2e638ad8fc0cfcb524: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5500"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 6</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.6.1-Ps.6.10">Psa 6:1-10</reference>. On Neginoth (See on <reference osisRef="Ps.4.1">Psa 4:1</reference>, title) upon Sheminith--the eighth--an instrument for the eighth key; or, more probably, the bass, as it is contrasted with Alamoth (the treble, <reference osisRef="Ps.46.1">Psa 46:1</reference>) in <reference osisRef="1Chr.15.20">1Ch 15:20</reference>,<reference osisRef="1Chr.15.21">21</reference>. In deep affliction the Psalmist appeals to God's mercy for relief from chastisement, which otherwise must destroy him, and thus disable him for God's service. Sure of a gracious answer, he triumphantly rebukes his foes.</title> <div sID="gen8344" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5500"/>1. He owns his ill desert in begging a relief from chastisement. <div eID="gen8344" type="x-p"/>

entries.5376bfc0f60d989a3e33c4710f593549366c1da1: <div eID="gen18445" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen18446" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18447" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18447" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen18446" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen18448" type="x-p"/> This Psalm contains a deprecation of eternal vengeance, <reference osisRef="Psa.6.1">Psa 6:1</reference>; a petition to God for mercy, <reference osisRef="Psa.6.2">Psa 6:2</reference>. This is enforced from a consideration of the psalmist's sufferings, <reference osisRef="Psa.6.3">Psa 6:3</reference>; from that of the Divine mercy, <reference osisRef="Psa.6.4">Psa 6:4</reference>; from that of the praise and glory which God would fail to receive if man were destroyed, <reference osisRef="Psa.6.5">Psa 6:5</reference>; from that of his humiliation and contrition, <reference osisRef="Psa.6.6">Psa 6:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.6.7">Psa 6:7</reference>. Being successful in his supplication, he exults in God, <reference osisRef="Psa.6.8">Psa 6:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.6.9">Psa 6:9</reference>; and predicts the downfall of all his enemies, <reference osisRef="Psa.6.10">Psa 6:10</reference>. <div eID="gen18448" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18449" type="x-p"/> This Psalm has the following inscription: To the chief Musician on Neginoth, upon Sheminith, A Psalm of David; which the Chaldee translates, "To be sung on neginoth, a harp of eight strings." The various interpretations given to this inscription, both by ancients and moderns, show us that nothing is known concerning it. We have already seen that neginoth probably signifies all instruments which emitted sounds by strokes, or stringed instruments in general. This Psalm was to be accompanied with such instruments; but one of a particular kind is specified, viz., sheminith; so called from its having eight strings. The chief musician is directed to accompany the recital of this Psalm with the above instrument. <div eID="gen18449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18450" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen18450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18451" type="x-p"/> O Lord, rebuke me not - This Psalm, Which is one of the seven Penitential Psalms, is supposed to have been written during some grievous disease with which David was afflicted after his transgression with Bath-sheba. It argues a deep consciousness of sin, and apprehension of the just displeasure of God. It is the very language of a true penitent who is looking around for help, and who sees, as Bishop Horne well expresses it, "above, an angry God, ready to take vengeance; beneath, the fiery gulf, ready to receive him; without, a world in flames; within, the gnawing worm." Of all these, none so dreadful as an angry God; his wrath he particularly deprecates. God rebukes and chastens him, and he submits; but he prays not to be rebuked in anger, nor chastened in hot displeasure. because he knows that these must bring him down to total and final destruction.
entries.3ffeeda87e516da807d9cd3b4c21d1090dc9047c: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen18451" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18452" type="x-p"/> Have mercy - I have no merit. I deserve all I feel and all I fear. <div eID="gen18452" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18453" type="x-p"/> O Lord, heal me - No earthly physician can cure my malady. Body and soul are both diseased, and only God can help me. <div eID="gen18453" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18454" type="x-p"/> I am weak - אמלל umlal. I am exceedingly weak; I cannot take nourishment, and my strength is exhausted. <div eID="gen18454" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18455" type="x-p"/> My bones are vexed - The disease hath entered into my bones.
entries.a99f7e94e80a8b242f8ea5e778afa1209599b230: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen18455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18456" type="x-p"/> How long? - How long shall I continue under this malady? How long will it be before thou speak peace to my troubled heart?
entries.f13ddea9e01c3af36a28a03cb001404dfca94658: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen18456" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18457" type="x-p"/> Return, O Lord - Once I had the light of thy countenance, by sin I have forfeited this; I have provoked thee to depart: O Lord, return! It is an awful thing to be obliged to say, Return, O Lord, for this supposes backsliding; and yet what a mercy it is that a backslider may Return to God, with the expectation that God will return to him!
entries.8bdd1889f1fbd10bd544c17aff02e6b916fddc72: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen18457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18458" type="x-p"/> In death there is no remembrance of thee - Man is to glorify thee on earth. The end for which he was born cannot be accomplished in the grave; heal my body, and heal my soul, that I may be rendered capable of loving and serving thee here below. A dead body in the grave can do no good to men, nor bring any glory to thy name!
entries.3930214b33a3b7ccb725fd7289297d2a83362b06: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen18458" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18459" type="x-p"/> Mine eye is consumed - עששה asheshah, is blasted, withered, sunk in my head.
entries.563d8db290df2b76779e8890fb2b3bfdbdd9cd85: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen18459" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18460" type="x-p"/> Depart from me, all ye workers of iniquity - It seems that while he was suffering grievously through the disease, his enemies had insulted and mocked him; - upbraided him with his transgressions, not to increase his penitence, but to cast him into despair. <div eID="gen18460" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18461" type="x-p"/> The Lord hath heard the voice of my weeping - The Lord pitifully beheld the sorrows of his heart, and mercifully forgave his sins.
entries.a8304de0e3ec90fbc59c868276d46d28ce93cefc: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen18461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen18462" type="x-p"/> Ashamed and sore vexed - May they as deeply deplore their transgressions as I have done mine! May they return; may they be suddenly converted! The original will bear this meaning, and it is the most congenial to Christian principles.  <chapter eID="Ps.6"/> <div eID="gen18462" type="x-p"/>

entries.d340137dcfb111d144c3f7a91463245d8e4ad243: <div eID="gen9080" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">A Cry for Mercy under Judgement</title> <div sID="gen9081" type="x-p"/> The morning prayer, <reference osisRef="Ps.5.1-Ps.5.12">Psa 5:1-12</reference>, is followed by a <hi type="italic">“Psalm of David,”</hi> which, even if not composed in the morning, looks back upon a sleepless, tearful night. It consists of three strophes. In the middle one, which is a third longer than the other two, the poet, by means of a calmer outpouring of his heart, struggles on from the cry of distress in the first strophe to the believing confidence of the last. The hostility of men seems to him as a punishment of divine wrath, and consequently (but this is not so clearly expressed as in Ps 38, which is its counterpart) as the result of his sin; and this persecution, which to him has God’s wrath behind it and sin as the sting of its bitterness, makes him sorrowful and sick even unto death. Because the Psalm contains no confession of sin, one might be inclined to think that the church has wrongly reckoned it as the first of the seven (probably selected with reference to the seven days of the week) <hi type="italic">Psalmi paenitentiales</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.6.1">Psa 6:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1">Psa 32:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.1">Psa 38:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.51.1">Psa 51:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.1">Psa 102:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.130.1">Psa 130:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.143.1">Psa 143:1</reference>). A. H. Francke in his <hi type="italic">Introductio in Psalterium</hi> says, it is rather <hi type="italic">Psalmus precatorius hominis gravissimi tentati a paenitente probe distinguendi</hi>. But this is a mistake. The man who is tempted is distinguished from a penitent man by this, that the feeling of wrath is with the one perfectly groundless and with the other well-grounded. Job was one who was tempted thus. Our psalmist, however, is a penitent, who accordingly seeks that the punitive chastisement of God, as the just God, may for him be changed into the loving chastisement of God, as the merciful One. <div eID="gen9081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9082" type="x-p"/> We recognise here the language of penitently believing prayer, which has been coined by David. Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.6.2">Psa 6:2</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.38.2">Psa 38:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.6.3">Psa 6:3</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.41.5">Psa 41:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.6.5">Psa 6:5</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.109.26">Psa 109:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.6.6">Psa 6:6</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.30.10">Psa 30:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.6.7">Psa 6:7</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.69.4">Psa 69:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.6.8">Psa 6:8</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.31.10">Psa 31:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.6.10">Psa 6:10</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.35.4">Psa 35:4</reference>, Psa 35:26. The language of Heman’s Psalm is perceptibly different, comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.6.6">Psa 6:6</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.88.11-Ps.88.13">Psa 88:11-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.6.8">Psa 6:8</reference> with Psa 88:10. And the corresponding strains in Jeremiah (comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.6.2">Psa 6:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.2">Psa 38:2</reference> with <reference osisRef="Jer.10.24">Jer 10:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.6.3">Psa 6:3</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.6.5">Psa 6:5</reference> with <reference osisRef="Jer.17.14">Jer 17:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.6.7">Psa 6:7</reference> with <reference osisRef="Jer.45.3">Jer 45:3</reference>) are echoes, which to us prove that the Psalm belongs to an earlier age, not that it was composed by the prophet (Hitzig). It is at once probable, from the almost anthological relationship in which Jeremiah stands to the earlier literature, that in the present instance also he is the reproducer. And this idea is confirmed by the fact that in <reference osisRef="Jer.10.25">Jer 10:25</reference>, after language resembling the Psalm before us, he continues in words taken from Psa 79:6. When Hitzig maintains that David could no more have composed this disconcertedly despondent Psalm than Isaiah could the words in <reference osisRef="Isa.21.3-Isa.21.4">Isa 21:3-4</reference>, we refer, in answer to him, to <reference osisRef="Isa.22.4">Isa 22:4</reference> and to the many attestations that David did weep, <reference osisRef="2Sam.1.12">2Sa 1:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.3.32">2Sa 3:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.12.21">2Sa 12:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2Sa 15:30</reference>; 2Sa 19:1. <div eID="gen9082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9083" type="x-p"/> The accompanying musical direction runs: <hi type="italic">To the Precentor, with accompaniment of stringed instruments, upon the Octave.</hi> The lxx translates ὑπὲρ τῆς ὀγδόης, and the Fathers associate with it the thought of the octave of eternal happiness, ἡ ὀγδόη ἐκείνη, as Gregory of Nyssa says, ἥτίς ἐστιν ὁ ἐφεξῆς αἰών. But there is no doubt whatever that על־השּׁמינית has reference to music. It is also found by <reference osisRef="Ps.12.1-Ps.12.8">Psa 12:1-8</reference>, and besides in 1Ch 15:21. From this latter passage it is at least clear that it is not the name of an instrument. An instrument with eight strings could not have been called an <hi type="italic">octave</hi> instead of an <hi type="italic">octachord</hi>. In that passage they played upon nablas על־עלמות, and with citherns על־השּׁמינית. If עלמות denotes maidens = maidens’ voices i.e., <hi type="italic">soprano</hi>, then, as it seems, השּׁמינית is a designation of the bass, and על־השׁמינית equivalent to <hi type="italic">all' ottava bassa</hi>. The fact that <reference osisRef="Ps.46.1-Ps.46.11">Psa 46:1-11</reference>, which is accompanied by the direction על־עלמות, is a joyous song, whereas <reference osisRef="Ps.6.1-Ps.6.10">Psa 6:1-10</reference> is a plaintive one and <reference osisRef="Ps.12.1-Ps.12.8">Psa 12:1-8</reference> not less gloomy and sad, accords with this. These two were to be played in the lower octave, that one in the higher. <div eID="gen9083" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9084" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Ps.6.1-Ps.6.3">Psa 6:1-3</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_6:2-4) There is a chastisement which proceeds from God’s love to the man as being pardoned and which is designed to purify or to prove him, and a chastisement which proceeds from God’s wrath against the man as striving obstinately against, or as fallen away from, favour, and which satisfies divine justice. <reference osisRef="Ps.94.12">Psa 94:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.17">Psa 118:17</reference>; Pro 3:11. speak of this loving chastisement. The man who should decline it, would act against his own salvation. Accordingly David, like Jeremiah (<reference osisRef="Jer.10.24">Jer 10:24</reference>), does not pray for the removal of the chastisement but of the chastisement in wrath, or what is the same thing, of the judgment proceeding from wrath [<hi type="italic">Zorngericht</hi>]. בּאפּך and בּחמתך stand in the middle, between אל and the verbs, for the sake of emphasis. Hengstenberg indeed finds a different antithesis here. He says: “The contrast is not that of chastisement in love with chastisement <hi type="italic">in wrath</hi>, but that of loving rescue in contrast with chastisement, which always proceeds from the principle of wrath.” If what is here meant is, that always when God chastens a man his wrath is the true and proper motive, it is an error, for the refutation of which one whole book of the Bible, viz., the Book of Job, has been written. For there the friends think that God is angry with Job; but we know from the prologue that, so far from being angry with him, he on the contrary glories in him. Here, in this Psalm, assuming David to be its author, and his adultery the occasion of it, it is certainly quite otherwise. The chastisement under which David is brought low, has God’s wrath as its motive: it is punitive chastisement and remains such, so long as David remains fallen from favour. But if in sincere penitence he again struggles through to favour, then the punitive becomes a loving chastisement: God’s relationship to him becomes an essentially different relationship. The evil, which is the result of his sin and as such indeed originates in the principle of wrath, becomes the means of discipline and purifying which love employs, and this it is that he here implores for himself. And thus Dante Alighieri<note placement="foot">Provided he is the author of <hi type="italic">I sêtte Salmi</hi> <hi type="italic">Penitenziali trasportati alla volgar poesia, </hi>vid., Dante Alighieri’s Lyric poems, translated and annotated by Kannegiesser and Witte (1842) i. 203f., ii. 208f.</note> correctly and beautifully paraphrases the verse:<hi type="italic">Signor, non mi riprender con furore, E non voler correggermi con ira, Ma con dolcezza e con perfetto amore</hi>. <div eID="gen9084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9085" type="x-p"/> In חנּני David prays God to let him experience His loving-kindness and tender mercy in place of the punishment He has a right to inflict; for anguish of soul has already reduced him to the extreme even of bodily sickness: he is withered up and weary. אמלל has <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi>, and consequently seems to be the <hi type="italic">3 pers. Pul</hi>. as in <reference osisRef="Joel.1.10">Joe 1:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.1.4">Nah 1:4</reference>; but this cannot be according to the rules of grammar. It is an adjective, like רענן, שׁאנן, with the passive pointing. The formation אמלל (from אמל Arab. <hi type="italic">aml</hi>, with the primary meaning to stretch out lengthwise) is analogous to the IX and XI forms of the Arabic verb which serve especially to express colours and defects (Caspari §59). The two words אני אמלל have the double accent <hi type="italic">Mercha-Mahpach</hi> together, and according to the exact mode of writing (vid., Baer in my <hi type="italic">Psalter</hi> ii. 492) the <hi type="italic">Mahpach</hi>, (the sign resembling <hi type="italic">Mahpach</hi> or rather <hi type="italic">Jethib</hi>), ought to stand between the two words, since it at the same time represents the <hi type="italic">Makkeph</hi>. The principal tone of the united pair, therefore, lies on <hi type="italic">aani</hi>; and accordingly the adj. אמלל is shortened to אמלל (cf. אדמדּם, הפכפּך, מרמס, and the like) - a contraction which proves that אמלל is not treated as <hi type="italic">part. Pul</hi>. (= מאמלל), for its characteristic <hi type="italic">a4</hi> is unchangeable. The prayer for healing is based upon the plea that his bones (<reference osisRef="Job.4.14">Job 4:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.38.13">Isa 38:13</reference>) are affrighted. We have no German word exactly corresponding to this נבהל which (from the radical notion “to let go,” cogn. בּלהּ) expresses a condition of outward overthrow and inward consternation, and is therefore the effect of fright which disconcerts one and of excitement that deprives one of self-control.<note placement="foot">We have translated Dr. Delitzsch’s word <hi type="italic">erschrecht</hi> literally - the <hi type="italic">vexed</hi> of the Authorized Version seems hardly equal to the meaning.</note> <div eID="gen9085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9086" type="x-p"/> His soul is still more shaken than his body. The affliction is therefore not a merely bodily ailment in which only a timorous man loses heart. God’s love is hidden from him. God’s wrath seems as though it would wear him completely away. It is an affliction beyond all other afflictions. Hence he enquires: And Thou, O Jahve, how long?! Instead of אתה it is written את, which the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> says is to be read אתּה, while in three passages (Num 11:15; <reference osisRef="Deut.5.24">Deu 5:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.14">Eze 28:14</reference>) אתּ is admitted as <hi type="italic">masc</hi>.
entries.39a8c209cff255e04e0002214ed1020009781f95: <reference osisRef="Ps.6.4-Ps.6.7">Psa 6:4-7</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_6:5-8) God has turned away from him, hence the prayer שׁוּבה, viz., אלי. The tone of שׁוּבה is on the <hi type="italic">ult</hi>., because it is assumed to be read שׁוּבה אדני. The <hi type="italic">ultima</hi> accentuation is intended to secure its distinct pronunciation to the final syllable of שׁובה, which is liable to be drowned and escape notice in connection with the coming together of the two aspirates (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.3.8">Psa 3:8</reference>). May God turn to him again, rescue (חלּץ from חלץ, which is transitive in Hebr. and Aram., to free, <hi type="italic">expedire, exuere,</hi> Arab. <hi type="italic">chalaṣa</hi>, to be pure, prop. to be loose, free) his soul, in which his affliction has taken deep root, from this affliction, and extend to him salvation on the ground of His mercy towards sinners. He founds this cry for help upon his yearning to be able still longer to praise God, - a happy employ, the possibility of which would be cut off from him if he should die. זכר, as frequently הזכּיר, is used of remembering one with reverence and honour; הודה (from ודה) has the <hi type="italic">dat. honoris</hi> after it. שׁאול, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.6.6">Psa 6:6</reference></hi>, ἅδης (<reference osisRef="Rev.20.13">Rev 20:13</reference>), alternates with מות. Such is the name of the grave, the yawning abyss, into which everything mortal descends (from שׁאל = שׁוּל Arab. <hi type="italic">sâl</hi>, to be loose, relaxed, to hang down, sink down: a sinking in, that which is sunken in,<note placement="foot">The form corresponds to the Arabic form <hi type="italic">fi‛âlun</hi>, which, though originally a verbal abstract, has carried over the passive meaning into the province of the concrete, e.g., <hi type="italic">kitâb</hi> = <hi type="italic">maktûb</hi> and <hi type="italic">ilâh</hi>, אלוהּ = <hi type="italic">ma‛lûh</hi> = <hi type="italic">ma‛bûd</hi> (the feared, revered One).</note> a depth). The writers of the Psalms all (which is no small objection against Maccabean Psalms) know only of one single gathering-place of the dead in the depth of the earth, where they indeed live, but it is only a <hi type="italic">quasi life</hi>, because they are secluded from the light of this world and, what is the most lamentable, from the light of God’s presence. Hence the Christian can only join in the prayer of v. 6 of this Psalm and similar passages (<reference osisRef="Ps.30.10">Psa 30:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.11-Ps.88.13">Psa 88:11-13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.115.17">Psa 115:17</reference>; Isa 38:18.) so far as he transfers the notion of hades to that of gehenna.<note placement="foot">An adumbration of this relationship of Christianity to the religion of the Old Testament is the relationship of Islam to the religion of the Arab wandering tribes, which is called the “religion of Abraham” <hi type="italic">( Din Ibrâhim ),</hi> and knows no life after death; while Islam has taken from the later Judaism and from Christianity the hope of a resurrection and heavenly blessedness.</note> <div eID="gen9086" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9087" type="x-p"/> In hell there is really no remembrance and no praising of God. David’s fear of death as something in itself unhappy, is also, according to its ultimate ground, nothing but the fear of an unhappy death. In these “pains of hell” he is wearied with (בּ as in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.4">Psa 69:4</reference>) groaning, and bedews his couch every night with a river of tears. Just as the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. השׂחה signifies to cause to swim from שׂחה to swim, so the <hi type="italic">Hiph</hi>. המסה signifies to dissolve, cause to melt, from מסה (cogn. מסס) to melt. דּמעה, in Arabic a <hi type="italic">nom. unit</hi>. a tear, is in Hebrew a flood of tears. <div eID="gen9087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9088" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Ps.6.8">Psa 6:8</reference> עיני does not signify my “appearance” (Num 11:7), but, as becomes clear from <reference osisRef="Ps.31.10">Psa 31:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.88.10">Psa 88:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.17.7">Job 17:7</reference>, “my eye;” the eye reflects the whole state of a man’s health. The verb עשׁשׁ appears to be a denominative from עשׁ: to be moth-eaten.<note placement="foot">Reuchlin in his grammatical analysis of the seven Penitential Psalms, which he published in 1512 after his Ll. III <hi type="italic">de Rudimentis Hebraicis</hi> (1506), explains it thus: עשׁשׁה <hi type="italic">Verminavit. Sic a vermibus dictum qui turbant res claras puras et nitidas, and in the Rudim.</hi> p. 412: <hi type="italic">Turbatus est a furore oculus meus, corrosus et obfuscatus, quasi vitro laternae obductus.</hi></note> <div eID="gen9088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9089" type="x-p"/> The signification <hi type="italic">senescere</hi> for the verb עתק is more certain. The closing words בּכל־צוררי (cf. Num 10:9 הצּר הצּרר the oppressing oppressor, from the root צר Arab. <hi type="italic">tsr</hi>, to press, squeeze, and especially to bind together, <hi type="italic">constringere, coartare</hi><note placement="foot">In Arabic ציר <hi type="italic">dir</hi> is the word for a step-mother as the oppressor of the step-children; and צרר <hi type="italic">dirr</hi>, a concubine as the oppressor of her rival.)</note>, in which the writer indicates, partially at least, the cause of his grief (כּעס, in <reference osisRef="Job.18.7">Job 18:7</reference> כּעשׁ), are as it were the socket into which the following strophe is inserted.
entries.69b7f1705fd421adf986b06aa4a07eee7a4af18e: <reference osisRef="Ps.6.8-Ps.6.10">Psa 6:8-10</reference> (Hebrew_Bible_6:9-11) Even before his plaintive prayer is ended the divine light and comfort come quickly into his heart, as Frisch says in his <hi type="italic">“Neuklingende Harfe Davids.”</hi> His enemies mock him as one forsaken of God, but even in the face of his enemies he becomes conscious that this is not his condition. Thrice in <reference osisRef="Ps.6.9">Psa 6:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.10">Psa 6:10</reference> his confidence that God will answer him flashes forth: He hears his loud sobbing, the voice of his weeping that rises towards heaven, He hears his supplication, and He graciously accepts his prayer. The twofold שׁמע expresses the fact and יקח its consequence. That which he seems to have to suffer, shall in reality be the lot of his enemies, viz., the end of those who are rejected of God: they shall be put to shame. The בּושׁ, Syr. <hi type="italic">behet</hi>, Chald. בּהת, בּהת, which we meet with here for the first time, is not connected with the Arab. <hi type="italic">bht</hi>, but (since the Old Arabic as a rule has <hi type="italic">t`</hi> as a mediating vowel between ש and <hi type="italic">t</hi>, )ת with Arab. <hi type="italic">bât</hi>, which signifies “to turn up and scatter about things that lie together (either beside or upon each other)” <hi type="italic">eruere et diruere, disturbare,</hi> - a root which also appears in the reduplicated form Arab. <hi type="italic">bṯṯ</hi>: to root up and disperse, whence Arab. <hi type="italic">battun</hi>, sorrow and anxiety, according to which therefore בּושׁ (= בּושׁ as Arab. <hi type="italic">bâta</hi> = <hi type="italic">bawata</hi>) prop. signifies <hi type="italic">disturbare</hi>, to be perplexed, lose one’s self-control, and denotes shame according to a similar, but somewhat differently applied conception to <hi type="italic">confundi</hi>, συγχεῖσθαι, συγχύνεσθαι. ויבּהלוּ points back to <reference osisRef="Ps.6.2">Psa 6:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.6.3">Psa 6:3</reference> : the lot at which the malicious have rejoiced, shall come upon themselves. As is implied in יבשׁוּ ישׁבוּ, a higher power turns back the assailants filled with shame (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.4">Psa 9:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.35.4">Psa 35:4</reference>). <div eID="gen9089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9090" type="x-p"/> What an impressive finish we have here in these three <hi type="italic">Milels , jashûbu jebôshu rāga )</hi>, in relation to the tripping measure of the preceding words addressed to his enemies! And, if not intentional, yet how remarkable is the coincidence, that shame follows the involuntary reverse of the foes, and that יבשׁו in its letters and sound is the reverse of ישׁבו! What music there is in the Psalter! If composers could but understand it!!  <chapter eID="Ps.6"/> <div eID="gen9090" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 6.
David, being afflicted by the hand of God, acknowledges that he had provoked the Divine wrath by his sins, and, therefore, in order to obtain relief, he prays for forgiveness. At the same time, he regrets, that by being taken out of the world, he would be deprived of an opportunity of praising God. Then, having obtained confidence, he celebrates the grace of God, and directs his discourse to his enemies, who triumphed over his calamities.
To the chief musician on Neginoth, upon the eighth. A song of David.
The name of Song shows that David composed this psalm, in which he describes the passionate workings of his grief in the time of his troubles after he had obtained deliverance from the evils which he deplores. What the kind of chastisement was of which he speaks is uncertain. Those who restrict it to bodily disease do not adduce in support of their opinion any argument of sufficient weight. They insist on the word אמל, amal, which occurs in verse third, where he says, “I am weak,” which indeed signifies to be sick; but it is more probable that it is here used metaphorically. They allege that Hezekiah, after his recovery from sickness, sung in the same strains as are here recorded, concerning death. But in <19B601>Psalm 116, where no mention is made of bodily disease, the same complaint is uttered by the Psalmist in the name of the whole Church. We can, indeed, gather from these words that the life of David was in the utmost danger, but it may have been some other kind of affliction than bodily sickness under which he labored. We may, therefore, adopt this as the more certain interpretation, that he had been stricken by some severe calamity, or that some punishment had been inflicted upon him, which presented to his view on every side only the shadow of death. It ought also to be considered, that this psalm was not composed at the very time when he presented to God the prayers recorded in it; but that the prayers which he had meditated and uttered in the midst of his dangers and sadness were, after he had obtained respite, committed to writing. This explains why he joins the sorrow with which he certainly had struggled for a time with the joy which he afterwards experienced. With respect to the word eighth, as we have before said that נגינות, Neginoth, signifies a musical instrument, I do not know whether it would be correct to say, that it was a harp of eight strings. I am rather inclined to the opinion that it refers to the tune, and points out the particular kind of music to which the psalm was to be sung.
Sheminith, or the eighth, “is thought to be the shrillest or loftiest note, as Alomoth is the lowest; of which see 1 Chronicles 15:20, 21. But all this is only conjecture; and the Jews themselves have no certain knowledge of their ancient music, and of the signification of the terms belonging to it.” — Poole’s Annotations.
However, in a matter so obscure and of so little importance I leave every one at liberty to form his own conjecture.
Psalm 6:1
1. Jehovah, rebuke me not in thine anger, and chastise me not in thine indignation.
 
The calamity which David now experienced had, perhaps, been inflicted by men, but he wisely considers that he has to deal with God. Those persons are very unsuitably exercised under their afflictions who do not immediately take a near and a steady view of their sins, in order thereby to produce the conviction that they have deserved the wrath of God. And yet we see how thoughtless and insensible almost all men are on this subject; for while they cry out that they are afflicted and miserable, scarcely one among a hundred looks to the hand which strikes. From whatever quarter, therefore, our afflictions come, let us learn to turn our thoughts instantly to God, and to acknowledge him as the Judge who summons us as guilty before his tribunal, since we, of our own accord, do not anticipate his judgment. But as men, when they are compelled to feel that God is angry with them, often indulge in complaints full of impiety, rather than find fault with themselves and their own sins, it is to be particularly noticed that David does not simply ascribe to God the afflictions under which he is now suffering, but acknowledges them to be the just recompense of his sins. He does not take God to task as if he had been an enemy, treating him with cruelty without any just cause; but yielding to him the right of rebuking and chastening, he desires and prays only that bounds may be set to the punishment inflicted on him. By this he declares God to be a just Judge in taking vengeance on the sins of men.
“En faisant vengence des forfaits des hommes.” — Fr.
But as soon as he has confessed that he is justly chastised, he earnestly beseeches God not to deal with him in strict justice, or according to the utmost rigour of the law. He does not altogether refuse punishment, for that would be unreasonable; and to be without it, he judged would be more hurtful than beneficial to him: but what he is afraid of is the wrath of God, which threatens sinners with ruin and perdition. To anger and indignation David tacitly opposes fatherly and gentle chastisement, and this last he was willing to bear. We have a similar contrast in the words of Jeremiah, (Jeremiah 10:24,) “O Lord,” says he, “correct me, but with judgment; not in thine anger.” God is, indeed, said to be angry with sinners whenever he inflicts punishment upon them, but not in the proper and strict sense, inasmuch as he not only mingles with it some of the sweetness of his grace to mitigate their sorrow, but also shows himself favorable to them, in moderating their punishment, and in mercifully drawing back his hand. But, as we must necessarily be stricken with terror whenever he shows himself the avenger of wickedness, it is not without cause that David, according to the sense of the flesh, is afraid of his anger and indignation. The meaning therefore is this: I indeed confess, O Lord, that I deserve to be destroyed and brought to nought; but as I would be unable to endure the severity of thy wrath, deal not with me according to my deserts, but rather pardon my sins, by which I have provoked thine anger against me. As often, then, as we are pressed down by adversity, let us learn, from the example of David, to have recourse to this remedy, that we may be brought into a state of peace with God; for it is not to be expected that it can be well or prosperous with us if we are not interested in his favor. Whence it follows, that we shall never be without a load of evils, until he forgive us our sins.
Psalm 6:2-3
2. Have mercy upon me, O Jehovah, for I am weak; heal me, O Jehovah, for my bones are afraid. 3. And my soul is exceedingly troubled;
Or greatly terrified. This is a very correct rendering of the original words נבהלה מאד; nibhalah meod: and they are very like those uttered by the Savior in his agony, “My soul is exceeding sorrowful, even unto death.”
and thou, O Jehovah, how long?
“Mais toy, Seigneur, jusques a quand m’affligeras-tu?” — Fr. “But thou, O Lord, how long wilt thou afflict me?”
